analysis.one_liner: Caps Senate campaign spending, bans unregulated party money, and eliminates leadership PACs.
analysis.headline: A campaign finance bill with two Democratic sponsors received one committee hearing in May 2000 and never came to a Senate vote before the 106th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have set mandatory spending limits for Senate campaigns, banned 'soft money' — the unregulated money that national party committees could raise and spend outside normal contribution limits — treated coordinated outside spending as a regular contribution, barred federal officeholders from running 'leadership PACs', and given the Federal Election Commission stronger enforcement tools, including random audits, injunctions, and larger penalties. The bill's stated purpose was to reduce the influence of large donors and the constant fundraising pressure on officeholders. It was referred to the Senate Rules and Administration Committee, which held a hearing in May 2000, and it never advanced further.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters and ordinary citizens, according to the bill's own findings, which note that fewer than 3 percent of citizens contribute to campaigns yet receive apparent favored access to lawmakers. Non-wealthy candidates would also benefit: mandatory spending caps would limit the advantage of wealthy self-funding opponents, and the cap automatically rises if outside groups outspend it against a candidate. Candidates and officeholders freed from constant fundraising would gain time for governing, the bill argues.

how_it_helps.text: Sets a cap on what a Senate candidate and their committee may spend per election — roughly $1.18 million or a formula based on state population, adjusted for inflation, with separate lower caps for primaries and runoffs.

Bans national party committees from soliciting, receiving, or spending soft money, and requires state and local party committees to fund any activity affecting a federal election with regulated 'hard money'.

Closes evasion channels: coordinated spending counts as a contribution, independent expenditures are capped and trigger a matching increase in the candidate's own limit, and federal officeholders are barred from maintaining any political committee besides their principal campaign committee — eliminating leadership PACs.

Strengthens enforcement by letting the FEC seek injunctions, conduct random post-election audits, expedite complaints filed within 60 days of an election, raise the penalty for knowing and willful violations, and bar contributions from people not qualified to vote in federal elections.

analysis.who_pays: National party committees and their major donors would lose the soft-money channel. Incumbent senators with large fundraising operations, wealthy candidates who self-finance, and operators of leadership PACs would face new limits. Broadcasters and political media firms would sell fewer campaign ads under capped spending, and campaigns would take on added reporting and compliance work.

drawbacks.text: The bill's own findings concede that the Supreme Court's Buckley v. Valeo decision 'disapproved the use of mandatory spending limits', so the central provisions — mandatory candidate spending caps and a cap on independent expenditures by any person — rested on weak constitutional ground. The bill even writes fallback rules to take effect 'when the limit is not in effect', an implicit acknowledgment that courts might strike the limits down.

Spending caps can restrict a campaign's ability to communicate. The bill tries to offset this by raising a candidate's limit in response to outside spending against them, but a hard cap on independent expenditures (Section 204) would directly restrict political speech by groups and individuals, the strongest good-faith objection to the bill.

The bill imposes new reporting, filing, and certification obligations on campaigns, party committees, and other groups spending on election activity, adding administrative cost and paperwork to political participation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's substance — a soft money ban, spending limits, and real enforcement teeth — goes well beyond the reforms that eventually passed in 2002, and its core spending caps carried genuine constitutional risk that the bill itself admits. The enforcement and reporting provisions are routine. On the merits it was an ambitious anti-corruption bill whose main defect was legal fragility, not bad design for ordinary people.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Rules and Administration Committee for the rest of the Congress — one hearing in May 2000 and no markup, no floor vote, and it died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Sen. Jack Reed introduced the bill on August 5, 1999, joined by Sen. Tim Johnson as its only cosponsor; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Rules and Administration.
The committee held a hearing on the bill on May 17, 2000, but took no further action on it.
No vote was ever scheduled in the full Senate, and the bill expired with the 106th Congress on January 3, 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: National party committees, their large donors, and incumbent senators kept the soft-money system and unlimited fundraising advantages through the 2000 elections; the only major campaign finance law of the era (2002) was narrower than this bill's mandatory spending limits.

for.name: Sen. Jack Reed
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Campaign Spending Control Act of 1999 and delivered introductory remarks.

for.name: Sen. Tim Johnson
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, its only cosponsor.

against.name: Senate Committee on Rules and Administration
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over election law
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral in August 1999, held a hearing in May 2000, and never reported it out for a floor vote.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.role: Senate Majority Leader and leadership, 106th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled campaign finance legislation, including this bill, for a Senate vote; the broader soft-money reform bill failed procedural votes requiring 60 senators twice in 1999.

sides.party_line_note: Both sponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on; the parallel fight over the broader McCain-Feingold soft-money bill in the same Senate split largely by party, with Republican leaders blocking floor action and a 1999 procedural vote failing 53-47.

industries.industry: National and state political party committees
industries.note: The bill bans national parties from raising or spending unregulated soft money but preserves a state-level role through 'State Party Grassroots Funds' with elevated contribution limits ($20,000 versus $5,000 for other state party committees). Parties' interest in unregulated money ran against the public's interest in disclosure and contribution limits.

industries.industry: Large individual donors and campaign contributors
industries.note: The bill's findings identify the small share of the population (under 3 percent) providing sizable contributions as receiving apparent favored access; the soft money ban and contribution rules would shrink that channel.

The spending cap applies to all candidate expenditures, including personal wealth, ending the effectively unlimited personal spending the bill's findings describe as forcing opponents into a fundraising arms race.

Section 206 bars federal officeholders from maintaining any political committee besides their principal campaign committee, forcing existing leadership PACs to disburse their funds within a year — a direct hit to incumbent fundraising and influence networks.
Capped campaign spending and capped independent expenditures would reduce political advertising revenue, though the cap rises in response to outside spending against a candidate.
